title: Forget Likes, This Social Media Contest Is All About the Crunch
summary:
Social media often gets a bad rap, but this week it's being used for an undeniably wholesome purpose: celebrating the crunch. Zoos around the United States are posting close-up videos of tree kangaroos noisily chomping on vegetables as part of the International Tree Kangaroo Crunch-a-Thon. The competition, organized by the conservation initiative AZA SAFE (Saving Animals From Extinction): Tree Kangaroo of Papua New Guinea, aims to draw attention to these lesser-known, tree-dwelling marsupials before World Tree Kangaroo Day on May 21.

Tree kangaroos belong to the genus Dendrolagus and are the only arboreal kangaroos. With 14 species spread across Australia, Indonesia, and Papua New Guinea, they sport bushy tails, long arms, and padded hind feet adapted for life in the canopy. Many are threatened by habitat loss and hunting; the golden-mantled tree kangaroo is one of the world's most endangered mammals, restricted to a tiny area of Papua New Guinea. The Crunch-a-Thon invites facilities working with tree kangaroos to post videos on Instagram or Facebook, with categories for Most Likes, Most Views, and Judges' Choice. Organizers even recommend crunchy foods — bell peppers, celery, romaine hearts, snap peas, green beans — while noting that cucumbers and zucchini "might not have the best crunch."

Roger Williams Park Zoo, home to three Matschie's tree kangaroos, joined in with a video of the pink-nosed marsupials munching enthusiastically. "In partnership with the AZA Tree Kangaroo SAFE program, we're participating in the Tree Roo Crunch-a-Thon to help shine a spotlight on this endangered species," the zoo posted. The contest cleverly turns the internet's love of cute animal content into a conservation tool. As the organizers put it, "let the crunching begin!" Winners will be announced on May 17, Australian Eastern Standard Time, so there's still time to scroll, smile, and maybe learn something about a creature you've never heard of before.
why_it_matters: Conservation contests like this show how digital media can mobilize public support for protecting lesser-known species critical to biodiversity, potentially slowing extinction rates.

background_read: Tree kangaroos are marsupials that evolved from ground-dwelling ancestors to live in trees, developing strong forelimbs, long tails, and padded feet for gripping branches. They belong to the genus Dendrolagus, with 14 species scattered across Australia, Indonesia, and Papua New Guinea.

Papua New Guinea, a nation occupying the eastern half of the island of New Guinea, is one of the most biodiverse yet underreported regions on Earth. The Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA, a nonprofit accreditor of zoos in North America) runs the SAFE program (Saving Animals From Extinction) to focus conservation efforts on specific endangered species.

The tree kangaroo SAFE program raises awareness and funds to protect these animals from habitat loss due to logging and slash-and-burn agriculture, as well as hunting. The Crunch-a-Thon, a lighthearted social media contest, is part of a global effort to celebrate World Tree Kangaroo Day on May 21, drawing attention to creatures many people have never seen.

perspectives.description: The Crunch-a-Thon creatively harnesses social media's reach to educate millions about an obscure endangered species. This could drive donations, inspire zoo visits, and even influence policy support for habitat protection.

Some argue that feel-good campaigns oversimplify conservation, distracting from the complex political and economic drivers of habitat loss in Papua New Guinea. Cute videos alone won't stop logging or empower local communities.

Tree kangaroos exemplify convergent evolution, showing how marsupials adapted to arboreal life much like monkeys did on other continents. They help scientists study how different lineages solve the same ecological challenges.

If the contest succeeds, similar online campaigns could be launched for other 'forgotten' species, using viral content to combat the extinction crisis. The model could link zoo breeding programs with global digital engagement.
